newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Port Arthur struggles to keep massacre site open.
newsitem.headline: Port Arthur struggles to keep massacre site open.

text.p: Australia's Port Arthur tourist site, where 35 people were shot dead a year ago, is struggling to remain open with many staff too disturbed to work.
Next Monday marks the first anniversary of the April 28 massacre, reviving traumatic memories of the shootings.
"We are battling to keep the site open," an emotional Craig Coombs, chief executive of the Port Arthur Historic Site, told Reuters on Thursday.
With the anniversary a few days away, many staff who were on duty on April 28 and who had returned to work over the past year were now finding it difficult, he said.
"We have still got a large number of staff who have been personally affected and are finding it difficult to deal with," said Coombs, himself a witness to the carnage.
Martin Bryant, a 29-year-old social misfit, committed modern Australia's worst mass murder when he opened fire with semi-automatic weapons on a busy Sunday afternoon at the site.
He is now serving life in prison without parole.

Port Arthur, a harsh penal colony in the last century, was until the massacre a popular tourist attraction in the remote southeast corner of the island state of Tasmania. It has for the past year tried to return to some normalcy, welcoming visitors.
Of the 22 staff who were working on April 28, about half have slowly returned to their old jobs, Coombs said.
But in recent days, as the tragedy's first anniversary approaches, the families of the dead have laid floral wreaths and homemade crosses at spots where loved ones died.
The gestures have served as disturbing reminders to staff. "It wears the staff pretty thin," said Coombs.
A church service will be held in the ruins of Port Arthur's old church on Monday morning to remember the victims. The service will be televised nationwide.
